plan: SAT R&W batch 64: 10 new items on new passages CLD-P-SAT-RW-000572..000581 (Wardenclyffe WIC, Timbuktu manuscripts inference, bee-visit quantitative evidence, chinampa cross-text, Ellen Swallow Richards purpose, Barracoon colon, Benin Bronzes agreement, Their Eyes Were Watching God transition, Clotilda synthesis, Whitman quotation evidence). Topics checked against every bank and the combined bank. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: An unfinished tower
passages.text: In the early 1900s, Nikola Tesla began building Wardenclyffe Tower on Long Island, a tall structure he hoped would transmit messages, and eventually electric power, without wires. His plans for the tower remained ______: after his financier, J. P. Morgan, withdrew support, construction stopped, and the tower was torn down in 1917.

passages.title: Saving the manuscripts
passages.text: Timbuktu, in present-day Mali, holds hundreds of thousands of manuscripts on subjects from astronomy to law, many kept for centuries in family libraries. When armed militants occupied the city in 2012, librarians led by Abdel Kader Haidara secretly packed most of the manuscripts into footlockers and moved them to Bamako, the capital. Before leaving in early 2013, the militants set fire to several thousand manuscripts at a research institute in the city. These events suggest that ______

passages.title: Bee visits
passages.text:
A student counted bee visits to blue and yellow flowers in a garden on one day.
Morning: blue 48 visits, yellow 16 visits
Afternoon: blue 30 visits, yellow 30 visits
The student claims that the bees' preference for blue flowers weakened over the day.

passages.title: Gardens on the lake
passages.text:
Text 1
Spanish accounts of Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, described its chinampas as "floating gardens," a phrase that still appears in many modern descriptions of the city's farms.

Text 2
Archaeologists note that chinampas did not float. Farmers built them by piling layers of lake mud and decaying vegetation inside fenced plots in shallow water, then planted willow trees along the edges, whose roots anchored the plots to the lake bed. The result was fertile, stable ground surrounded by canals.

passages.title: Mapping the water
passages.text: In 1887, the chemist Ellen Swallow Richards led a survey for the Massachusetts State Board of Health that analyzed tens of thousands of water samples from across the state. From the results she drew a map showing how chlorine levels in water rose near the coast and in populated areas, where sewage raised them. The map gave officials a baseline for judging whether a water supply had been polluted, and the survey led to some of the first water-quality standards in the United States.

passages.title: A life in three parts
passages.text: Zora Neale Hurston's Barracoon, based on her interviews in 1927 and 1928 with Cudjo Lewis, tells the story of his life in three ______ his childhood in West Africa, his capture and transport to Alabama on the ship Clotilda, and his decades of life afterward in a community near Mobile.

passages.title: Returning the bronzes
passages.text: The collection of more than 1,100 Benin Bronzes held by German museums, many of which British soldiers had taken from the royal palace in Benin City in 1897, ______ transferred to Nigerian ownership in 2022.

passages.title: A rediscovered novel
passages.text: Zora Neale Hurston's novel Their Eyes Were Watching God received mixed reviews when it was published in 1937, and by the time Hurston died in 1960, it was out of print. ______ after Alice Walker's 1975 essay "In Search of Zora Neale Hurston" renewed interest in her work, the novel was reissued and became a staple of American literature courses.

passages.title: Notes on a ship
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Clotilda was the last known ship to bring enslaved Africans to the United States, arriving in Alabama in 1860, decades after the trade was outlawed.
- After the voyage, the ship was burned to hide evidence of the crime.
- Many of the people it carried later founded Africatown, a community near Mobile.
- Descendants of those people still live in Africatown.
- In 2019, researchers confirmed that a wreck in the Mobile River was the Clotilda.

passages.title: A lecture and the night sky
passages.text: "When I Heard the Learn'd Astronomer" is an 1865 poem by Walt Whitman. In the poem, the speaker suggests that direct experience of nature is more meaningful to him than a scientific explanation of it.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: construction stopped, and the tower was torn down in 1917
candidates.explanation: Plans for a tower that was never finished and was later torn down were never carried out, or "unrealized."

A.rationale: Nothing in the text suggests the plans were ordinary; they were ambitious.

B.rationale: The project lost its funding and was abandoned, so it made no profit.

C.rationale: The text does not suggest the plans were hidden.

candidates.remember: Use the explanation after the colon to define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the militants destroyed most of Timbuktu's manuscripts before leaving.
choices.B: without the evacuation, the losses would likely have been far greater.
choices.C: the manuscripts were safer in Timbuktu than they would have been in Bamako.
choices.D: the manuscripts had never been studied before they were moved to Bamako.

candidates.evidence: secretly packed most of the manuscripts into footlockers
candidates.explanation: The militants burned the manuscripts they could reach; because most had been moved, the evacuation likely prevented much greater losses.

A.rationale: Several thousand were burned, but most had already been moved.

C.rationale: The manuscripts left behind were the ones burned.

D.rationale: The text says nothing about earlier study.

hints: What happened to the manuscripts that stayed behind?

strategy.explanation: Compare what was moved with what was burned.

candidates.remember: An inference should follow from the facts the text gives.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the student's claim?

choices.A: Blue flowers drew 75% of visits in the morning but only 50% in the afternoon.
choices.B: Blue flowers received 48 visits in the morning and 30 in the afternoon.
choices.C: Yellow flowers received 30 visits in the afternoon, the same number as blue flowers.
choices.D: The bees made 64 visits in the morning and 60 in the afternoon.

candidates.evidence: the bees' preference for blue flowers weakened over the day
candidates.explanation: Preference is a share of visits: 48 of 64 (75%) in the morning versus 30 of 60 (50%) in the afternoon.

B.rationale: Blue visits fell, but total visits also changed, so this alone does not show a weaker preference.

C.rationale: This describes the afternoon only and makes no comparison with the morning.

D.rationale: Totals say nothing about which color was preferred.

hints: How can you measure preference fairly?
candidates.remember: A preference is a proportion, not a raw count.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the archaeologists in Text 2 most likely respond to the description in Text 1?

choices.A: They would agree that the gardens floated but say they were less fertile than described.
choices.B: They would argue that the Spanish never saw chinampas in Tenochtitlan.
choices.C: They would say the gardens were fixed in place rather than floating.
choices.D: They would say that chinampas were built on dry land far from the lake.

candidates.explanation: Text 2 explains that chinampas were built up from the lake bed and anchored by willow roots, so the "floating" description is inaccurate.

A.rationale: They reject the idea that the gardens floated and call them fertile.

B.rationale: Text 2 does not question whether the Spanish saw chinampas.

D.rationale: Text 2 says chinampas were built in shallow water.

hints: What part of Text 1's description does Text 2 dispute?

strategy.explanation: Find the specific claim Text 2 corrects.

candidates.remember: A response may reject one detail rather than the whole account.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To argue that Richards deserves more credit than other chemists of her time
choices.B: To describe a scientific survey and explain how its results were put to use
choices.C: To explain how sewage enters water supplies near the coast
choices.D: To compare water-quality standards in Massachusetts and other states

candidates.evidence: the survey led to some of the first water-quality standards
candidates.explanation: The text describes Richards's survey and map, then explains how officials used them as a baseline and how the survey led to water-quality standards.

A.rationale: The text does not compare her with other chemists.

C.rationale: The text mentions sewage only to explain the chlorine pattern.

D.rationale: The text does not compare states' standards.

hints: What do the last two sentences add?
candidates.remember: A purpose answer should cover the whole text.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: A colon after the complete clause "tells the story of his life in three stages" correctly introduces the list of three stages.

B.rationale: A semicolon cannot introduce a list.

C.rationale: A colon should not follow "such as."

D.rationale: Without punctuation, the list runs directly into the clause.

hints: Is the part before the list a complete clause?

strategy.explanation: Check what can introduce a list.

candidates.remember: Use a colon after a complete clause to introduce a list.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: The collection of more than 1,100 Benin Bronzes
candidates.explanation: The subject is the singular "collection"; the plural nouns between it and the verb do not change that, so the verb is "was."

A.rationale: "Were" is plural, but the subject "collection" is singular.

B.rationale: "Have" is plural, but the subject "collection" is singular.

C.rationale: "Being" is not a finite verb, leaving the sentence without a main verb.

hints: What is the subject of the sentence?

strategy.explanation: Cross out the phrases between the subject and the verb.

candidates.remember: Collective nouns like "collection" take singular verbs.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.explanation: The text moves from 1960 to events after 1975, so a time transition marking a much later period fits.

A.rationale: The novel's later success is not an example of its earlier neglect.

B.rationale: The novel's revival contrasts with, rather than resembles, its fall from print.

D.rationale: The novel's going out of print did not cause its later revival.

hints: How much time passes between the two sentences?

strategy.explanation: Check the dates on each side of the blank.

candidates.remember: Use a time transition when the text jumps forward.

candidates.subskill: Rhetorical synthesis (emphasizing significance to a community)
candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize why the 2019 discovery mattered to Africatown's residents. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In 2019, researchers confirmed that a wreck in the Mobile River was the Clotilda, which had been burned in 1860.
choices.B: For Africatown residents, many descended from its captives, the 2019 discovery confirmed a long-hidden history.
choices.C: The Clotilda arrived in Alabama in 1860, decades after the trade in enslaved people was outlawed in the United States.
choices.D: Africatown, a community near Mobile, Alabama, was founded by people who had been brought to the United States.

candidates.evidence: Descendants of those people still live in Africatown
candidates.explanation: Only choice B links the discovery to the residents, many of whom descend from the people the ship carried.

A.rationale: This states the discovery but not why it mattered to Africatown.

C.rationale: This gives background but does not mention the residents or the discovery.

D.rationale: This describes the community but not the discovery.

hints: Which choice connects the discovery to the residents?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against the exact goal.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must address the goal's specific focus.

candidates.stem: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: "When the proofs, the figures, were ranged in columns before me, / When I was shown the charts and diagrams, to add, divide, and measure them,"
choices.B: "When I sitting heard the astronomer where he lectured with much applause in the lecture-room,"
choices.C: "How soon unaccountable I became tired and sick,"
choices.D: "I wander'd off by myself, / In the mystical moist night-air, and from time to time, / Look'd up in perfect silence at the stars."

candidates.evidence: direct experience of nature is more meaningful to him
candidates.explanation: The final lines show the speaker leaving the lecture to look at the stars in silence, which illustrates his preference for direct experience over explanation.

A.rationale: This describes the lecture but shows no preference for direct experience.

B.rationale: This describes the setting; the applause even suggests others valued the lecture.

C.rationale: This shows the speaker's discomfort with the lecture but not what he values instead.

hints: Which quotation shows both what he leaves and what he turns to?

strategy.explanation: Match each quotation to both parts of the claim.

candidates.remember: Choose the quotation that supports every part of the claim.
